For a differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y=0,
$$

we have that if

$$
\frac{1}{P}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})=h(y)
$$

where $h(y)$ is independent of $x,$ then an integrating factor for the equation is

$$
I(y)=\operatorname{exp}⁡(-\int h(y)\,\text{d}y).
$$

Let's denote

$$
P(x,y)=2{y}^{3},\,Q(x,y)=-xy.
$$

Now, let's compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{y}^{3})=6{y}^{2} \\ \frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-xy)=-y\end{aligned}
$$

Since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{P}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x}) & =\frac{1}{2{y}^{3}}(6{y}^{2}-(-y)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2{y}^{3}}(6{y}^{2}+y) \\  & =\frac{6y+1}{2{y}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

is a function of $y$ only, we can conclude that an integrating factor for our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}I(y) & =\operatorname{exp}⁡(\int -\frac{6y+1}{2{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =\operatorname{exp}⁡(-(3\operatorname{ln}⁡y-\frac{1}{2y})) \\  & =\operatorname{exp}⁡(-3\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\cdot \operatorname{exp}⁡(\frac{1}{2y}) \\  & ={y}^{-3}{e}^{1/(2y)}.\end{aligned}
$$

and by multiplying our differential equation by the integrating factor, we have

$$
I(y)\cdot (2{y}^{3}\,\text{d}x-xy\,\text{d}y)=0
$$

which simplifies as

$$
{y}^{-3}{e}^{1/(2y)}(2{y}^{3}\,\text{d}x-xy\,\text{d}y)=0.
$$
